title: Obtain Capabilities: Code Signing Certificates
summary: This sub-technique covers buying or stealing a code signing certificate, which is a certificate used to put a verifiable digital signature on software and scripts. The purpose is attribution of trust: a valid signature tells the operating system and the user that a named publisher produced the code and that nobody altered it afterwards. Adversaries want that appearance of legitimacy, because signed binaries are treated more leniently by security controls, are less likely to prompt a user warning, and sometimes survive application control policies that block unsigned code. Purchase is normally done through a front company, or by impersonating an entity whose records were previously stolen, so that identity validation with the certificate provider succeeds. The more disruptive path is theft: taking the private key and certificate from a compromised software vendor, build system, or certificate authority. Either way, the material is used before the signing step, and that signing step becomes its own technique. The defender signature for this behaviour is not a signature at all but a mismatch. A file may carry a valid chain while the publisher name has no relationship to the product, the signing time falls outside any plausible build window, or the certificate was issued to an entity with no business history. Certificate transparency logs, vendor revocation notices, and timestamp analysis help investigators date the compromise. Once abuse is suspected, revocation is the only reliable containment, and it affects every genuinely signed product from that publisher.

beginner.definition: A code signing certificate proves who made a program and that nobody changed it afterwards. This technique is about attackers buying or stealing one. They use it to make their harmful software look officially published.
beginner.whyItMatters: Computers and users trust signed software more than unsigned software. A stolen certificate lets malicious files pass checks that would normally stop them. The victim company whose certificate was stolen may also face serious damage when the certificate is cancelled.
howItWorks: The attacker applies for a certificate or looks for one to steal.
They hide their identity by using a fake company or a real company's stolen records.
The certificate provider validates the claimed identity and then issues the requested certificate.
Alternatively they steal the certificate and its private key from a software supplier.
They sign their own harmful programs so that the digital signature looks genuine.
Defenders notice when a signature does not match the product, and the certificate is revoked.
beginner.example: Imagine a museum that accepts deliveries only with a stamped company seal. A criminal obtains a real seal from a company that went out of business, or steals one from a delivery office. The wax looks perfect. Only when someone compares the seal to the company name on the box does the story fall apart.
takeaways: A valid signature proves a key was used, not that the software is safe.
Compare the publisher name with the product before you trust a signature.
Revoking a stolen certificate is the only sure fix, and it hurts the real owner.

objectives: Explain what a code signing certificate proves about a program.
Describe how adversaries obtain signing certificates through front companies or stolen identities.
Explain why a stolen signing certificate is more damaging than a forged one.
Recognise the mismatches that expose abuse of a legitimately issued certificate.
Explain the trade off of revoking a compromised signing certificate.
